2c(1).fact: Tilting the boat into the turn presents the hull bottom to the incoming current so the water flows underneath rather than catching the exposed upstream edge.
2c(1).misconception: Leaning away from the turn keeps the boat flatter and prevents tipping over when crossing an eddy line.
2c(1).pamphlet_summary: Crossing an eddy line requires tilting the canoe or kayak downstream into the turn so the bottom of the hull faces the incoming current. This hull angle allows opposing water flows to slide underneath the craft rather than catching the upstream gunwale or chine (p. 31).
2c(1).socratic_question: How does the angle of your hull determine whether conflicting water currents slip underneath your boat or flip it over?

2c(2).fact: Paddlers must always tilt the boat downstream so the oncoming river current slides under the hull rather than grabbing the upstream chine and swamping the craft.
2c(2).misconception: Upstream ferrying requires tilting the boat toward the upstream current to slice cleanly through incoming waves.
2c(2).pamphlet_summary: Paddlers must angle the boat across the river current and tilt the hull downstream during both upstream and downstream ferries. Presenting the bottom of the hull to the oncoming flow prevents the water from pushing against the upstream edge and swamping the boat (p. 32).
2c(2).socratic_question: Why must your boat always tilt downstream regardless of whether you are executing an upstream ferry or a downstream ferry?

4a(1).fact: Bow paddlers perform the cross bow draw by rotating the torso across the opposite gunwale while keeping their original paddle grip unchanged.
4a(1).misconception: Switching to an offside cross bow draw requires swapping top and bottom hand positions on the paddle shaft.
4a(1).pamphlet_summary: The bow paddler in a tandem canoe executes cross forward strokes, draws, pries, and sculling draws to guide the front of the craft around river obstacles. These strokes shift the bow laterally and accelerate the boat across eddy lines through coordinated body rotation and paddle placement (p. 42).
4a(1).socratic_question: How does rotating your torso across the boat without changing your paddle grip allow for faster directional corrections in heavy whitewater?

4a(2).fact: Active forward strokes ending in a stern pry maintain boat speed and provide far greater directional control than passive dragging rudders in moving current.
4a(2).misconception: Dragging the paddle blade passively behind the canoe like a rudder controls river maneuvers better than applying active stern pry strokes.
4a(2).pamphlet_summary: The stern paddler maintains directional heading and alters river trajectories using stern draws, pries, sculling draws, and forward strokes paired with a stern pry. These strokes provide continuous propulsion while enabling precise ruddering and turning adjustments from the back of the canoe (p. 44).
4a(2).socratic_question: Why does combining a forward stroke with an active stern pry keep a tandem canoe on course much better than simply dragging the blade behind the boat?

4a(3).fact: Keeping elbows low and pointing downward protects the shoulder joint from dislocation while applying downward pressure to right the canoe.
4a(3).misconception: Raising elbows high above the paddle shaft provides the greatest leverage when performing an emergency high brace.
4a(3).pamphlet_summary: Tandem paddlers prevent capsizes by deploying low braces on the back of the blade, high braces with down-turned elbows, and righting pries using the gunwale as a fulcrum. Applying pressure to the blade while rolling the hips underneath the body restores the canoe to an even keel (p. 46).
4a(3).socratic_question: Why is keeping your elbows pointed down beneath the paddle shaft essential for protecting your shoulders while recovering balance in rough water?

4b(1).fact: Solo paddlers maintain their standard hand grip and rotate their torso across the gunwale to execute efficient offside cross forward and cross draw strokes.
4b(1).misconception: Solo canoeists must swap their hand grip across the paddle when transitioning between onside draws and offside cross strokes.
4b(1).pamphlet_summary: A solo canoeist commands the entire craft from the center kneeling position by executing draws, cross draws, pries, and sculling motions on both sides of the hull. Rotating the torso across the gunwale permits powerful offside strokes without shifting paddle grip or losing forward trim (p. 50).
4b(1).socratic_question: How does executing strokes on the offside without switching your grip allow a solo canoeist to maneuver quickly in turbulent rapids?

4b(2).fact: Righting a canoe requires an active hip snap to roll the hull upright while the paddle blade provides only momentary surface support.
4b(2).misconception: Pushing down on the water surface with the paddle blade can right a heavily tilted canoe without moving the lower body.
4b(2).pamphlet_summary: Solo canoeists stabilize unstable hull angles through low braces, high braces, and gunwale-assisted righting pries in turbulent water. The paddler pairs blade support on the water surface with an active hip snap to pull the craft upright before balance is lost (p. 52).
4b(2).socratic_question: What role does your lower body play when using a paddle brace to pull a heavily leaned solo canoe back underneath your center of gravity?

4c(1).fact: Trailing the paddle blade near the stern with a slight outward angle lets moving water turn the kayak without stalling forward momentum.
4c(1).misconception: Wedging a stern rudder deeply under the kayak hull produces the sharpest turn in fast current.
4c(1).pamphlet_summary: Solo kayakers adjust boat angle and track across rapid features using bow draws ahead of the hips, trailing stern rudders, and active sculling draws. These strokes leverage the double-bladed paddle to pull the kayak sideways or turn the bow without arresting craft momentum (p. 56).
4c(1).socratic_question: How does adjusting the blade angle of a trailing stern rudder let moving current turn your kayak without draining your forward speed?

4c(2).fact: Keeping elbows bent and tucked inside the paddling box protects shoulder joints from dangerous dislocation while delivering maximum bracing leverage.
4c(2).misconception: Reaching both arms far out away from the kayak provides the most solid support during a high brace.
4c(2).pamphlet_summary: Kayakers recover from severe tilts in heavy whitewater by slapping the water surface with a low brace or pulling down on a high brace. Maintaining bent elbows inside the torso paddling box preserves shoulder stability while the lower body snaps the kayak upright (p. 58).
4c(2).socratic_question: Why does keeping your arms inside the paddling box give you better mechanical leverage and injury protection during an aggressive high brace?
